# MSX Sound Suite integration interface

> This is an English translation of the [Japanese original](../msse-abi.md). Where the two differ, the Japanese version is authoritative.

MSX Sound Suite Extension (MSSX) is a mechanism that puts several sound-chip extension ROMs on one cartridge and shows only one of them at a time in page 1 (`4000h`-`7FFFh`). This document defines the rules that participating ROMs and applications follow.

The assembly-side definitions are in `src/inc/msse.inc`, and the hardware bank layout is in [`hardware.md`](hardware.md).

## Participating ROMs

| ID | ROM | Bank | Repository |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 0 | MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 | #0, #1, part of #5 ([below](#id-0s-fmbios-body-goes-in-5)) | [MsxMusicBasicExtension](https://github.com/madscient/MsxMusicBasicExtension) |
| 1 | MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite | #2, #3 | [MsxAudioBasicExtensionLite](https://github.com/madscient/MsxAudioBasicExtensionLite) |
| 2 | Y8960 BASIC Extension | #4, #5, #10-#15 | this repository |
| 3 | OPM BASIC Extension | #6, #7 | [SFGBasicExtension](https://github.com/madscient/SFGBasicExtension) |
| 4 | MIDI Play BASIC Extension | #8, #9 | [MidiPlayBasicExtension](https://github.com/madscient/MidiPlayBasicExtension) |

OPM BASIC Extension is SFG BASIC Extension adapted to the Y8960's OPM, and is built from the same repository. It plays the OPM built into the cartridge, not an SFG-01/05 in another slot. What MIDI Play BASIC Extension plays is an external sound module connected to a MIDI interface in another slot, not the Y8960's sound chips.

**However, wherever its main sound chip is, a ROM that plays the internal PSG can also play the Y8960's SSGS.** The SSGS sits on the same ports as the internal PSG, so the registers the PSG driver writes reach it as they are. **A ROM that uses the SSGS takes on the obligation to write the [I/O Enabler](#io-enabler).** A ROM that does not use it uses none of the cartridge's I/O ports, so it takes on no obligation either. MIDI Play BASIC Extension has no PSG, so it does not have this option either.

A participating ROM does not have to be a BASIC extension. Only those that are BASIC extensions follow the section "[Additional rules for BASIC extensions](#additional-rules-for-basic-extensions)".

A ROM that keeps separate builds, one integrated as MSX Sound Suite and one sold as a standalone cartridge, **must not put anything this document defines in the standalone build**. Neither the signature nor the attach entry has any meaning when there is nothing to switch to, and they make applications malfunction.

## Bank allocation

The cartridge memory is 8KB×32 banks: #0-#15 are ROM and #16-#31 are RAM (bank RAM below). From the MSX, two windows are visible in page 1.

| Window | Address | What appears |
|---|---|---|
| BANK0 | `4000h`-`5FFFh` | The first half of the ROM that is switched in |
| BANK1 | `6000h`-`7FFFh` | The second half of the same ROM, or a bank that ROM swaps in and uses |

### The first-half bank number is fixed at ID×2

**ID×2 is the bank number of that ROM's first half.** This cannot be moved. The bank number to switch to cannot be read before switching (to read the other side's table, the other side must first be in BANK0), so it must be computable from the ID alone.

Therefore the even banks **#0 / #2 / #4 / #6 / #8 are reserved as the first halves of IDs 0-4**
and must not be used for anything else. MSX Sound Suite handles five IDs, 0-4.

At power-on and at reset, the initial values of the bank registers are BANK0=#0, BANK1=#1.
**So the ID 0 ROM is switched in at startup.** It is also the ROM an application sees first when it finds the cartridge.

### Second-half and additional banks

The second-half bank number is published in `XBT_BANK1` of `XBTAB`, so it does not have to be ID×2+1. The same goes for the additional banks used by a ROM larger than 16KB: **they are taken from the pool starting at #10**. The build that assembles the cartridge image decides the allocation of the pool.

### ID 0's FMBIOS body goes in #5

MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 puts its FMBIOS body, which does not fit in #0 and #1, at **the top of bank #5, the second half of Y8960 BASIC Extension**.

| Address in #5 | Owner |
|---|---|
| `6000h`-`77FFh` | The second half of Y8960 BASIC Extension |
| `7800h`-`7FDFh` | The FMBIOS body of MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 (2016 bytes) |
| `7FE0h`-`7FFFh` | Neither puts anything here. `FFh` |

While a ROM bank is in BANK1, Memory Mapped I/O appears from `7FF0h` upward ([`hardware.md`](hardware.md)), so the boundary is placed below it, at `7FE0h`.

- **The second half of Y8960 BASIC Extension cannot be moved from #5.** MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 holds as a constant the 5 it writes to BANK1 when entering the FMBIOS body. This is an exception, limited to ID 2, to "Second-half and additional banks" leaving the second-half bank number free
- **The body is produced by the MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 repository as `build/rom/mmbe_y8960_fmbios.bin`.** It is a raw 2048-byte image covering `7800h`-`7FFFh`, and from `7FE0h` onward it is `FFh`
- **The build that assembles the cartridge image places it at offset `1800h` of #5.** It verifies the size, that everything from `7FE0h` onward is `FFh`, and that the #5 side puts nothing from `7800h` onward

### Page 2 shows #5 at startup

At power-on and at reset, the initial value of BANK2 is #2, which holds the cartridge header of ID 1's first half. It starts with `'AB'`, and its STATEMENT is not 0.
The cartridge also responds in page 2 (`8000h`-`BFFFh`), so if left as it is, the BIOS slot scan finds this header and records that page 2 of the same slot has another set of extended statements. Then a `CALL` statement that no ROM in page 1 accepts is passed on to the page 2 record, and the STATEMENT address in the header is called. That address
is in page 1 and points into the middle of the code of whichever ROM is in page 1 at that moment.

- **ID 0's cartridge INIT sets RAM mode to 1 and writes 5 to `4FFEh` (BANK2).** The scan calls the INIT in page 1 before it reads page 2, so writing it inside INIT is in time. Once the scan is done, nobody reads the header in page 2, so it is not restored
- **Do not make the first 2 bytes of #5 `'AB'`.** #5 is the second half of Y8960 BASIC Extension, and it starts with a jump table. The build that assembles the cartridge image verifies this
- There are two reasons for using #5. A second-half bank does not need a header at its start. And #5's number is already fixed by the section above as ID 2's second half

## What each ROM provides

Only three addresses are fixed; everything else may be placed anywhere in the first half.

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `400Ah` | `dw XBTAB` |
| `4010h` | `db 'MSSE8960'` (8 bytes) |
| `4060h` | Attach entry |

`4061h`-`406Fh` are reserved for MSX Sound Suite. Future entries are appended at the end.

### `400Ah` — XBTAB pointer

The first 2 bytes of the 6 reserved bytes of the MSX cartridge header. `XBTAB` itself may be placed anywhere in the first half.

| Offset | Contents |
|--:|---|
| +0 | `'XB'` (2-byte signature) |
| +2 | This ROM's own ID |
| +3 | The bank number of this ROM's own second half |
| +4 | `jp ENTER` (the landing point of a BASIC extension; a ROM that is not one may use `ret`) |

### `4010h` — MSX Sound Suite signature

The 8 bytes `'MSSE8960'`. It is the marker by which an application finds the cartridge in a slot scan, and **all five ROMs carry the same one**. This is so that the cartridge is found whichever ROM is switched in. The 8-byte spelling is the one from when the ABI was frozen, and it does not change even if the way the product name is written changes.

The signature alone tells you only "something of MSX Sound Suite". Which ROM is switched in is told by `XBT_ID` in `XBTAB`.

### `4060h` — attach entry

Switches BANK0 to the ROM with the specified ID.

| | |
|---|---|
| Input | `A` = ID to switch to |
| Output | CY clear = that ROM's first half is now in BANK0<br>CY set = failure. BANK0 is as it was when called |
| Destroys | `AF` and the registers the implementation uses. `CALLSLT` itself destroys `IY` |

When `A` is its own ID, it writes its own [I/O Enabler](#io-enabler) without touching the bank registers and returns success. **This path is placed in the first half.**
It cannot be placed in the second half: as described later, when it is called in the middle of a switch, BANK1 is not its own second half.

When `A` is another ID, the procedure is as described in "[Switching order](#switching-order)".

There are two reasons for failure: the other side does not identify itself with `XBTAB` (an image without that bank), or the called side could not clean up after itself. **In either case BANK0 is unchanged, but the cleanup has already been done** (because cleanup is done before switching). The extended functions of the ROM you called are left stopped.

## RAM mode and bank registers

Before touching the bank registers, set RAM mode to 1 by writing 1 to `4FFBh`. This is the only address visible in both modes.

| | RAM mode 0 | RAM mode 1 |
|---|---|---|
| BANK0 | `5000h`-`57FFh` | `4FFCh` |
| BANK1 | `7000h`-`77FFh` | `4FFDh` |
| BANK2 | `9000h`-`97FFh` | `4FFEh` |

From then on, MSX Sound Suite uses only the RAM mode 1 side. Handing over page 1 writes `4FFCh` / `4FFDh`, and the only place this document specifies writing `4FFEh` is [ID 0 at startup](#page-2-shows-5-at-startup). This does not prevent the one that is switched in from writing the bank registers itself to swap bank RAM in and out ("[Using bank RAM](#using-bank-ram)"). **RAM mode is not restored.**

The bank registers are write-only and cannot be read. The switching side can switch back because it reads and keeps `XBT_ID` before switching; that ID×2 is the original value of BANK0.

## I/O Enabler

The Y8960 cartridge has its regular I/O ports disabled right after power-on and right after reset, and they become enabled only once the I/O Enabler in Memory Mapped I/O (`7FF6h` / `7FFFh`) is written. This mechanism lets multiple Y8960s be controlled individually, and follows the same idea as the Panasonic FMPAC. Details are in [`hardware.md`](hardware.md).

Therefore **a ROM that drives its sound chips through the regular I/O ports must write its own share of the I/O Enabler at the moment it is switched in.** It writes them in the attach entry's "addressed to itself" path and in a BASIC extension's `ENTER`. Only OPL2EX (bit0 of `7FFFh`) falls outside this practice ([below](#opl2ex-stays-enabled-from-startup)).

The I/O Enabler is memory-mapped into BANK1, so a ROM bank must be in BANK1 when it is written. On either path, a participating ROM's second half is there, so the condition is met.

**When handing over page 1, a ROM sets what it enabled back to 0.** The ports handed out here are the same ones the MSX computer uses for its own hardware (`A0h`/`A1h` are the PSG, `7Ch`/`7Dh` are MSX-MUSIC), so if they are left enabled, the cartridge's sound chips also respond to writes to them. OPL2EX, which appears on the MSX-AUDIO ports, is not set back, because making it respond is the purpose.

### SSGS coexists with the internal PSG

The SSGS ports `A0h`/`A1h` are the same as those of the internal PSG, and once they are enabled, both respond to writes to registers 0-15. **Even so, a ROM that uses the SSGS enables them.**

This is because the same sound merely comes out of two chips, which does no real harm. The SSGS is write-only and has no general-purpose I/O corresponding to `R14`/`R15` of the internal PSG, so it does not interfere with keyboard and joystick scanning. By rewriting only the volume and panning on the SSGS side along the way, both chips sounding can itself be used as a feature.

**A ROM that uses only the SSGS also gets nothing through unless it enables them.** The SSGS panning registers are at numbers the internal PSG does not decode, so on a machine without a Y8960, writes to them are discarded. That safety does not mean that the writes reach the SSGS on a machine with a Y8960: unless the Enabler is written, the cartridge answers on no port.

That there is no real harm is only the judgment of the side that enables them. **When handing over, the SSGS is also set back to 0.** The next ROM switched in does not necessarily use the SSGS, and the PSG of a ROM that does not use it would sound doubled for no reason.

### OPL2EX stays enabled from startup

**For the OPL2EX ports (`C0h`/`C1h`, bit0 of I/O Enabler 2), ID 0's cartridge INIT decides whether to enable them, and after that no ROM changes this.** No ROM enables them when it is switched in, and none sets them back when handing over.

This is for compatibility with the original MSX-AUDIO. An MSX-AUDIO cartridge responds on `C0h` from the moment the power is turned on, and some software drives the chip directly without going through the BASIC extension. If OPL2EX is there from startup, such software can play OPL2EX as an MSX-AUDIO. This has nothing to do with which ROM is switched in.

**ID 0's cartridge INIT** decides bit0 in the following order.

1. Set I/O Enabler 2 to 0. A warm boot does not reset the cartridge, so an OPL2EX enabled earlier may be on `C0h`
2. Probe whether an OPL-family chip is on `C0h`. As the MSX-AUDIO BIOS does, start timer 1 and see whether bit6 of the status changes from 0 to 1. Interrupts are disabled while probing
3. Stop the timer of the probed chip. If it were stopped after enabling, the writes that stop it would reach OPL2EX
4. If none is there, set bit0 to 1. If one is there, leave it at 0

INIT enables only bit0; it does not enable bit7 (TIMER). OPL2EX timer interrupts do not reach the MSX computer while bit7 is disabled ("Interrupts" in [`hardware.md`](hardware.md)), so they reach it only while a ROM that enables bit7 is switched in.

**When writing `7FFFh` anywhere other than INIT, first read `7FFFh`, and write bit0 back as read.** This applies both when enabling on being switched in and when setting back on handing over. For the other bits, do not use the value read; decide them yourself. `7FFFh` is the only readable register among the Enablers, and it is read with a ROM bank in BANK1, just as when it is written. `7FF6h` (I/O Enabler 1) has no such exception.

**The case where another chip holds `C0h` (use together with an MSX-AUDIO cartridge) is not assumed.** In that case OPL2EX does not appear on the regular I/O ports, and what a ROM that plays OPL2EX writes to `C0h` reaches that chip.

## Digital Mixer

The cartridge has only one Digital Mixer, with volumes for the master and five blocks (SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX, SCC, OPM). Its registers are in the Memory Mapped I/O of BANK1; for all six, 0 is mute and 128 is maximum, and the reset value is 128 ([`hardware.md`](hardware.md)).

"ROMs that play the cartridge's sound chips" here means the four ROMs with IDs 0-3. MIDI Play BASIC Extension does not play the cartridge's sound chips, so it does not carry the obligations of this section.

### The receiving side initializes it

**A ROM that plays the cartridge's sound chips sets all six mixer registers to 128 at the moment it is switched in.** It writes them in the same places as the I/O Enabler: the attach entry's "addressed to itself" path and a BASIC extension's `ENTER`. On either path, a participating ROM's second half is in BANK1, so the registers are visible.

**The side handing over page 1 has no obligation to restore the mixer.** Whatever the previous owner left behind, the receiving side puts the mixer in the default state itself. This is because the receiving side cannot tell whether the previous owner touched the mixer.

**ID 0 also sets all six to 128 in its cartridge INIT.** On a warm boot without a reset, the mixer keeps the values the previous owner left, and no switch happens either. ID 0's INIT is always passed through before a conventional application that uses the MSX-MUSIC FMBIOS as is starts. The INITs of the other ROMs do not initialize the mixer. At INIT time, a ROM bank is not necessarily in BANK1, so ID 0 switches in its own second half before writing.

The initialization and termination statements of a BASIC extension do not touch the mixer. It is touched only at the moment a ROM is switched in and by the `CALL MIXER` that follows.

### `CALL MIXER` works whichever ROM is switched in

A BASIC extension that plays the cartridge's sound chips has `CALL MIXER` in its build integrated as MSX Sound Suite. It is not a switch trigger; **the ROM that is switched in executes it itself.**

`CALL MIXER(master, SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX, SCC, OPM)`

- None of the six arguments can be omitted. Each is 0-128
- The values are written to the registers as they are: the master to `7FFEh`, the four blocks from SSGS to SCC to `7FF7h`-`7FFAh`, and OPM to `7FFDh`. No other register is written
- If even one is out of range, it is an `Illegal function call` error, and nothing is written to the mixer
- The initialization statement does not have to have been executed first

The mixer values return to 128 when the ROM that is switched in changes (if the new one is MIDI Play BASIC Extension, they stay as they are). There is no way to carry the values over across a switch.

### Applications use the BIOS

Applications are recommended not to write the mixer registers directly, but to use `SQMIX` of Y8960 BASIC Extension ([`sequencer-bios.md`](sequencer-bios.md)). **Attaching any of IDs 0-3 sets all six back to 128**, so make the settings after attaching ID 2.

## Cleaning up before handing over

**The side handing over page 1 forcibly terminates its own extended functions before handing over.** If the ROM disappears with its hooks still set, then at the next interrupt, whatever happens to be at that address in the destination ROM is executed. Users and applications are not required to terminate explicitly.

At a minimum: releasing the interrupt hooks, returning the allocated work area, and setting the I/O Enabler back (except bit0 of OPL2EX; [above](#opl2ex-stays-enabled-from-startup)).

**Returning the work area includes setting the `SLTWRK` entry back to 0.** `SLTWRK` is looked up by slot and page, so the participating ROMs in page 1 of the same slot **all share one 2-byte entry**. If a ROM hands over while leaving its pointer there, the next ROM switched in reads it as its own and concludes that it has a work area of its own, even though it has not run yet. This is not merely a leak of your own.

Using this entry as a presence flag is fine, but **it must be back to 0 when handing over.**

If someone took `H.TIMI` after you did, removing your hook drops that party from the chain, and there is no way to restore it. **In this case, do not clean up; refuse the switch.**

## Using bank RAM

Bank RAM is **occupied entirely by whoever is switched in at that time.** The one switched in may decide what to use it for and how much. Therefore, as a rule, information that persists beyond a switch must not be placed in bank RAM. A ROM that uses bank RAM does any necessary initialization on its own responsibility.

While it is switched in, it may let third-party applications use bank RAM. When it lets an application use bank RAM, the one switched in decides the contract appropriately.

## Switching order

Neither the first half nor the second half can page itself out. `4FFCh` is inside the BANK0 window, so the moment it is written, the code doing the writing disappears. Therefore a switch takes the form of the first half and the second half handing over to each other in turn.

1. **The first-half code** cleans up after itself and switches its own second half into BANK1
2. **Jump to the second half**
3. **The second-half code** sets RAM mode to 1 and writes ID×2 to `4FFCh`, switching BANK0 to the destination's first half. The running code is in the second half, so it does not disappear
4. The second-half code reads the destination's `XBTAB` from `400Ah` and checks `'XB'` and `XBT_ID`. If they do not match, it writes its own ID×2 to `4FFCh` to go back, and returns failure
5. Pass control to the destination. **There are two ways to pass it**

**BANK1 may or may not be switched.** Whether the destination's second half is switched in depends on the way control is passed.

### When handing over from the attach entry

`call` the destination's `4060h` with `A` = the destination's ID, and when it returns, `ret` to the application. The destination enters its "addressed to itself" path and writes its own I/O Enabler.

**At this point, BANK1 is left holding the called side's second half.** The destination's second half is not switched in. The destination needs its own second half when it starts running, and it can switch it in itself at that point. This is why the "addressed to itself" path of the destination's `4060h` must be in the first half: if it were in the second half, the jump would land on the same address in the called side's second half.

### When handing over to a BASIC extension's ENTER

Jump to the `jp ENTER` at `XBTAB+4`. `ENTER` is in the destination's first half; there, it switches the value of `XBT_BANK1` into BANK1 and then carries on. It does not return.

## Additional rules for BASIC extensions

Participating ROMs that have MSX BASIC `CALL` extended statements also follow the rules below.

### What triggers a switch

A switch happens on a statement whose name the switched-in ROM knows but whose body it does not have.

| Statement | Destination |
|---|---|
| `CALL MUSIC` | MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 |
| `CALL AUDIO` | MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite |
| `CALL MINIT` | Y8960 BASIC Extension |
| `CALL OPM` | OPM BASIC Extension |
| `CALL MIDI` | MIDI Play BASIC Extension |

Each participating BASIC extension has the names of all the others in its statement name table, and its handlers for them hand over page 1 **without reading any arguments**. The arguments are read when the destination ROM executes the statement from its own table. The `(-1)` in `CALL MUSIC(-1)` is interpreted by MSX-MUSIC, not by the side that handed over.

### The text pointer is passed in DE

**The BASIC text pointer is passed in `DE`, not in `HL`.**
The second-half code loads the address of the destination's `ENTER` into `HL` and jumps with `JP (HL)`, so the text pointer cannot be left in `HL`.

- The second-half code of the handing-over side moves the text pointer to `DE` with `EX DE,HL` before using `HL`, and does not destroy `DE` after that (it cannot be written as adding `XBT_ENTER` with `LD DE,4`; use a row of `INC HL`)
- The destination's `ENTER`, after switching BANK1, puts the text pointer back into `HL` with `EX DE,HL` and then jumps to the statement handler
- When returning because the signature does not match, the code likewise restores `HL` with `EX DE,HL`, and then returns with CY set

`PROCNM` is in BASIC's work area, so it is left as it is. If the statement is redispatched by name, the destination ROM reads the arguments.

### Rebuilding the work area

A BASIC extension that lowers `HIMEM` to take a work area needs to have BASIC's file buffers and string area, which lie below it, rebuilt. **The cleanup when handing over page 1 does not rebuild them.** It only returns its own block, and the next side to allocate rebuilds them once.

## Use from applications

The procedure for use from outside BASIC (MSX-DOS, ROM cartridges, etc.).

1. Follow `EXPTBL` / `SLTTBL` to select page 1 of every slot (including expanded slots) in turn, and look for a slot where `4000h` is `'AB'` and `4010h` is `'MSSE8960'`. Do not touch the bank registers
2. For the slot found, call `4060h` with `A` = the target ID using `CALLSLT` (`RST 30h`)
3. If CY is not set, the target ROM's first half is in BANK0. From then on, the entries that ROM publishes can be called with `CALLSLT` to the same slot

**The ROM holding page 1 when you call is not necessarily ID 0, the one switched in at startup.** In an application started from BASIC without an intervening reset, another ROM may be switched in. The signature is the same in all five, so the scan works in any state.

### Restrictions while a ROM that hooks interrupts is in use

**BANK0 must not be switched.** MSX interrupt hooks are called through the `RST 30h` inter-slot call, but `RST 30h` switches only the slot and does not touch the bank registers. If BANK0 is switched back to another ROM, then at the next interrupt, whatever happens to be at the hook address in that ROM is executed.

For the same reason, **BANK1 is also under that ROM's control**. An application must not switch BANK1 in and out on its own.

## When the other side does not answer

An image that lacks some of the participating ROMs may well be built. What is in a bank can be asked only after switching, so make sure you can go back.

The second-half code writes its own ID×2 to `4FFCh` to return BANK0 to itself, and returns with CY set. On the BASIC extension path, it must also remember to put the text pointer back into `HL`.

The build that assembles the cartridge image must verify the `XBTAB` of each bank it includes, and fail right there if an image that does not identify itself is mixed in. Noticing after running it is too late.
